title: Computer Arithmetic and Floating Point
subtitle: How computers store numbers, add, multiply and approximate fractions.

references.title: Arithmetic for Computers
references.topics: Signed and unsigned numbers, addition and subtraction, overflow, multiplication, division, floating point and IEEE 754

objectives: Represent unsigned and signed (two's complement) integers
Add and subtract binary numbers and detect overflow
Explain shift-and-add multiplication and restoring division
Explain the IEEE 754 single-precision fields and convert simple values
Explain why some decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly

steps.question: Two puzzles: why can adding two positive numbers give a negative result, and why is 0.1 + 0.2 not exactly 0.3?
clues: Computer numbers have a **fixed number of bits**, so they can run out of room.
Negative numbers share the same bit patterns as big positive ones.
Fractions are stored in binary, and some decimal fractions have **no finite binary form**.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: Unsigned binary integers

terms.note: each bit has a weight that doubles to the left

steps.why: A word has a fixed width, so every integer type has a smallest and a largest value.
steps.real: A 32-bit counter that adds 1 each millisecond wraps around after about 49 days.

explainAgain.beginner: A car odometer with 4 digits goes from 0000 to 9999, then rolls over to 0000. Binary registers do the same.

steps.title: Signed numbers: two's complement

items: The leftmost bit has a **negative** weight: −2ⁿ⁻¹
All other bits keep their positive weights
The leftmost bit is the **sign bit**: 1 means negative
n bits cover −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1 (8 bits: −128 to 127)

steps.why: One adder works for both signed and unsigned numbers; only the way we read the pattern changes.
steps.real: Java int, C int and MIPS words all use two's complement.

mistake.wrong: The leftmost bit is just a plus or minus sign and the rest is the magnitude.
mistake.right: In two's complement the leftmost bit carries weight −2ⁿ⁻¹, not a separate sign.

notes.explain: Read 11111011 both ways: 251 as unsigned, but −128 + 123 = −5 as signed.

steps.title: Negate: flip all the bits, add 1
steps.why: Press the negate button on 5: you get 11111011 = −5. Press it again and you are back at 5.

steps.question: What is the 8-bit pattern `11111011` as a signed number?

reveal.text: Leftmost bit weight −128; the other bits give 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 123. −128 + 123 = **−5**. (As unsigned it is 251.)

steps.result: Flip the bits (00000100) and add 1 (00000101) to get the magnitude 5.

steps.title: In MIPS: signed and unsigned comparison

blocks.title: Negation and slt vs sltu
blocks.hint: $t0 is −5. The nor/addi pair negates it. Compare slt (signed) with sltu (unsigned).

steps.why: The same bits give different answers: −5 < 0 for slt, but as unsigned it is a huge number, so sltu says no.
steps.real: Array bounds checks use unsigned comparison for exactly this reason.

steps.question: What is the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer?
steps.why: The sign bit has weight −128, so the lowest value is −128 and the highest is 127.
feedback: That range would give two zeros; two's complement has one.
8 bits give only 256 patterns in total.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each 8-bit pattern with its signed value.
steps.why: Negative numbers start with a 1 in the leftmost bit.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about two's complement is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. The leftmost bit of a negative number is 1.
2. Negating a number flips every bit and adds 1.
steps.explain: Two's complement has a single zero, which is one of its advantages.
steps.fix: There is only one zero (all bits 0).

questions.q: What weight does the leftmost bit have in an n-bit two's complement number?
How do you negate a two's complement number?
questions.a: Flip all the bits, then add 1.

questions.q: What is the range of a 32-bit signed integer?

steps.title: Binary addition

items: Add each column right to left: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=**10** (write 0, carry 1)
Each column also adds the carry from the column on its right
The same hardware adder works for signed and unsigned numbers
**Subtraction** a − b is a + (−b): negate b, then add

steps.why: Because of two's complement, subtraction needs no separate subtractor logic.
steps.real: Your CPU's ALU is built around exactly this: one adder, plus an inverter for subtraction.

steps.title: Try it: addition with carries
steps.why: 109 + 38 = 147 does not fit in 8 signed bits: watch the carries and the overflow flag.

steps.title: Overflow

head: Case
Unsigned detection
Signed detection
rows: A carry out of the top bit
Two operands with the same sign give a result of the opposite sign

steps.why: Overflow depends on how you interpret the bits, so signed and unsigned have different tests.
steps.real: An overflowed counter is behind many famous software bugs, from counters wrapping around to money errors.

mistake.wrong: Overflow happens whenever there is a carry out of the top bit.
mistake.right: A carry out signals unsigned overflow only; signed overflow needs the sign check.

deeper.text: Adding numbers of opposite sign can never overflow in two's complement.

steps.question: In 8-bit signed arithmetic, what is 109 + 38?

reveal.text: 109 + 38 = 147 is above 127, so the pattern 10010011 is read as **−109**. Two positive operands gave a negative result: signed overflow.

steps.result: The true sum 147 needs 9 signed bits.

steps.title: MIPS: add vs addu

left.title: add / addi / sub
items: Signed arithmetic
**Traps** (exception) on signed overflow
Used by languages that must detect overflow, such as Ada

right.title: addu / addiu / subu
items: Wraps around silently
No exception
Used for addresses and by C and Java integer arithmetic

steps.why: MIPS lets the programmer or compiler choose whether overflow is an error or is ignored.
steps.real: Java and C int addition wraps around (addu), so 2,147,483,647 + 1 gives −2,147,483,648.

steps.title: Run it: add vs addu

blocks.title: add traps on overflow
blocks.hint: The same addition with add stops with an arithmetic overflow error.

steps.why: Same operands, two instructions: one wraps, the other raises an exception.

steps.question: Which test detects overflow when adding two signed numbers?
options: Both operands have the same sign and the result has the opposite sign
There is a carry out of the top bit
steps.why: This is the signed overflow rule.
feedback: A carry out only indicates unsigned overflow.

steps.statement: Adding a positive and a negative two's complement number can overflow.
steps.why: Their sum always lies between the two operands, so it fits.

steps.title: Multiplication: shift and add

items: Look at each bit of the multiplier, from the right
If the bit is **1**, add the multiplicand to the product
Shift the multiplicand left by 1 each step (×2)
After n steps the product is complete

steps.why: A multiplication is a series of shifts and additions, the same as long multiplication in decimal.
steps.real: This 13 × 11 = 143 example takes four steps; a 32-bit multiply takes 32 steps in the simplest hardware.

explainAgain.beginner: Long multiplication on paper: each digit of the second number produces a shifted copy of the first.

steps.title: Try it: multiplication
steps.why: Change the multiplier to 9 or 15 and predict the partial products.

steps.title: The same in MIPS

blocks.title: 13 × 11 with sll, srl and add
blocks.program:
addi $s0, $zero, 13
addi $s1, $zero, 11
addi $s2, $zero, 0
addi $t0, $zero, 0
loop: slti $t1, $t0, 4
beq $t1, $zero, end
andi $t2, $s1, 1
beq $t2, $zero, skip
add $s2, $s2, $s0
skip: sll $s0, $s0, 1
srl $s1, $s1, 1
addi $t0, $t0, 1
j loop
end:
blocks.hint: $s2 collects the product, $s0 doubles each loop and $s1 loses its lowest bit each loop.

steps.why: This is the multiply algorithm written as a loop: and, test, add, shift.

steps.question: What does the MIPS loop leave in `$s2`?

reveal.text: The multiplier 11 = 1011 has bits 1, 1, 0, 1 (from the right), so it adds 13, 26 and 104: 13 + 26 + 104 = **143**.

steps.result: The 0 bit in position 2 means that step adds nothing.

steps.title: Division: restoring

items: Bring down one bit of the dividend into the remainder
Try to subtract the divisor
If the remainder stays ≥ 0, the quotient bit is **1**
Otherwise **restore** (undo) the subtraction and the quotient bit is **0**
Repeat for every bit

steps.why: Division is repeated trial subtraction. It is slower than multiplication, which is why compilers avoid it where they can.
steps.real: A 32-bit divide takes dozens of cycles on many processors, so programmers prefer shifts for dividing by powers of 2.

steps.title: Try it: division
steps.why: Watch each remainder step and the quotient bits appear.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Put one step of shift-and-add multiplication in order.
items: Look at the lowest bit of the multiplier
If it is 1, add the multiplicand to the product
Shift the multiplicand left by 1
Shift the multiplier right by 1
Repeat for the next bit
steps.why: The bit test comes first, and both shifts prepare the next step.

steps.question: What is the remainder of 13 ÷ 3?
steps.why: 13 = 3 × 4 + 1, so the quotient is 4 and the remainder is 1.
feedback: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor.

steps.title: Why floating point?

items: Integers cannot hold fractions or extremely large or small numbers
Scientific notation: ± 1.xxxx × 10ⁿ, with a **sign**, a **significand** and an **exponent**
The binary version is ± 1.xxxx₂ × 2ⁿ
IEEE 754 fixes how these are laid out so every computer agrees

steps.why: A float trades exactness for range: it can represent tiny and huge values using the same 32 bits.
steps.real: Games, graphics, science and machine learning all depend on floating point.

steps.title: IEEE 754 single precision

terms.note: it is not stored, which gives 24 bits of precision

steps.why: The bias lets the exponent be stored as an unsigned number, so floats can be compared with integer-style hardware.
steps.real: Java float and C float use exactly this layout.

mistake.wrong: The stored exponent is the real exponent.
mistake.right: The stored exponent is the real exponent plus 127.

steps.title: Worked example: 5.75
steps.why: This is the whole conversion procedure: binary, normalize, add the bias, fill the fields.

steps.title: Try it: IEEE 754 fields
steps.why: Type 5.75, then −6.5, 0.75, 100 and 0.1 and compare the fields with your hand conversion.

steps.question: What is the hexadecimal pattern of −6.5?
steps.result: The only difference from +6.5 (0x40D00000) is the sign bit.

steps.title: Special values
steps.why: Reserving the extreme exponents gives infinity and NaN, so computations such as 1/0 do not crash.
steps.real: NaN appears when you compute 0/0 or the square root of a negative number.

steps.title: Rounding: 0.1 is not exact

items: 0.1 = 0.0001100110011…₂: the binary expansion **never ends**
A float keeps only 24 significant bits, so it stores the nearest value
In single precision 0.1 is stored as 0x3DCCCCCD ≈ 0.10000000149
Whole numbers up to 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 are exact; 16,777,217 is not

steps.why: This is why comparing floats with == is risky: the stored values are approximations.
steps.real: Never use floats for exact money: use integers (cents) or decimal types.

mistake.right: It stores the nearest binary fraction, about 0.10000000149.

explainAgain.beginner: One third is 0.3333… in decimal and never ends. One tenth is the same kind of problem in binary.

steps.question: The exponent field of 1.0 in IEEE single precision is:
steps.why: Real exponent 0 plus the bias 127 gives 127 (0x3F800000).
feedback: 0 would be the real exponent before biasing.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: A float has 32 bits, the same as an int. Why can it store numbers up to about 3.4 × 10³⁸ while an int stops at about 2.1 billion?
steps.answer: The float spends its bits differently: 8 bits of exponent give it an enormous range, but only 24 bits of significand, so it can only keep about 7 significant decimal digits. It gains range and loses exactness.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: When should a program use integers instead of floating-point numbers?
ideas: Counters and indexes: use integers; floats lose exactness above 16,777,216.
Scientific measurements: floats are fine because the data are approximate anyway.
Comparisons: compare floats with a tolerance, not with ==.

questions.q: What are the three fields of IEEE 754 single precision?
questions.a: Sign (1 bit), exponent (8 bits, bias 127) and fraction (23 bits).
Its binary expansion never ends, so it is rounded to 24 bits.

questions.q: What does an exponent field of 255 mean?

steps.question: What is the range of a 4-bit unsigned integer, and of a 4-bit two's complement integer?
steps.solution: Four bits give 16 patterns. Unsigned 0 to 15; signed −2³ = −8 to 2³ − 1 = 7.

steps.question: Write −20 as an 8-bit two's complement number in binary and hex.
Add the 8-bit signed numbers 01101101 and 00100110. Give the result and say whether signed overflow occurred.
steps.solution: Add column by column with carries: the result is 10010011 = 147 unsigned, but as signed it is −109. Two positive operands gave a negative result.
steps.hint: Check the signs of the operands and the result.

steps.question: Convert 100 to IEEE 754 single precision (hex).
steps.hint: Normalize first, then add 127 to the exponent.
steps.mistake: Forgetting the bias, or storing the hidden 1.

steps.question: Add 200 and 100 as 8-bit numbers. What is the result and does unsigned overflow occur? Does signed overflow occur?
steps.answer: Result 44 with a carry out: unsigned overflow yes; signed overflow no.
steps.solution: 200 + 100 = 300 = 256 + 44, so the 8-bit result is 44 with a carry out (unsigned overflow). As signed: −56 + 100 = 44 with no sign problem (opposite signs).
steps.mistake: Using a carry out to claim signed overflow.
steps.title: Exam practice: numerical

steps.question: Multiply 13 by 11 with shift-and-add. Give the product after each of the four steps.
steps.solution: The multiplier bits from the right are 1, 1, 0, 1. Add 13; add 26; add 0; add 104. Running totals: 13, 39, 39, 143.
steps.mistake: Not shifting the multiplicand each step.
steps.title: Exam practice: numerical

steps.question: Divide 13 by 3 (4-bit restoring division). What are the quotient and remainder?
steps.solution: Go through the bits 1, 1, 0, 1 of 13, subtracting 3 whenever the remainder allows: quotient bits 0, 1, 0, 0 give 4; final remainder 1.
steps.title: Exam practice: numerical

steps.question: Explain why 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in a float, and why 16,777,217 cannot be stored exactly either.
steps.answer: In binary, 0.1 is a repeating fraction (0.000110011…), so it must be rounded to 24 significant bits. A float has only a 24-bit significand, so integers above 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 cannot all be represented; 16,777,217 is rounded to 16,777,216.
steps.solution: A strong answer mentions the finite significand in both cases.
steps.mistake: Saying the float runs out of exponent bits.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: n-bit unsigned: 0 to 2ⁿ−1. n-bit two's complement: −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹−1; negate = flip + 1.
Addition uses the same adder for signed and unsigned; subtraction adds the negation.
Signed overflow: same-sign operands, opposite-sign result. Unsigned overflow: a carry out of the top bit.
MIPS add traps on overflow; addu wraps around.
Multiplication is shift-and-add; division is repeated trial subtraction.
IEEE single: 1 sign, 8 exponent (bias 127), 23 fraction, hidden leading 1.
Floats are approximations: 0.1 is rounded and integers above 16,777,216 are not exact.

mistakes.wrong: The leftmost bit is only a sign.
mistakes.right: It has weight −2ⁿ⁻¹ in two's complement.

mistakes.wrong: A carry out always means overflow.
The stored float exponent is the real exponent.
mistakes.right: It is the real exponent plus 127.

mistakes.wrong: 0.1 is stored exactly in a float.
mistakes.right: It is stored as the nearest binary fraction.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Computers store integers in two's complement and fractions in IEEE 754. Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division all work on a fixed number of bits, so overflow and rounding are real effects. Signed overflow and unsigned overflow are detected differently, multiplication is shift-and-add, and floats approximate real numbers with sign, biased exponent and a 23-bit fraction.

questions.question: How many different values can 8 bits represent?

questions.statement: In two's complement a leading 1 means the number is negative.
questions.why: The sign bit has negative weight.
questions.misconception: The leftmost bit is 1 for every negative value.

questions.question: What is the exponent bias in IEEE 754 single precision?
questions.misconception: The field is 8 bits wide, so the bias is 2⁷ − 1.

questions.question: What is 11111011 as an 8-bit signed number?
questions.misconception: It is 251 only if read as unsigned.

questions.question: When does signed overflow occur in addition?
options: Same-sign operands give an opposite-sign result
Whenever there is a carry out
questions.why: That is the signed overflow rule.
questions.misconception: A carry out signals unsigned overflow.

questions.question: Which float is 0x3F800000?
questions.misconception: The exponent field 127 means a real exponent of 0.

questions.question: Which MIPS instruction wraps around silently on overflow instead of trapping?
questions.misconception: add, addi and sub raise an exception on signed overflow.

questions.question: A 32-bit float is asked to store 16,777,217. What does it actually hold?
questions.why: The 24-bit significand cannot represent 2²⁴ + 1, so it rounds to 16,777,216.
questions.misconception: Integers above 2²⁴ lose exactness in single precision.

items.q: Give the range of an n-bit two's complement integer.

items.a: Negate the second number (flip, add 1) and add.

items.q: What are the steps of shift-and-add multiplication?
items.a: Test the multiplier bit, add the multiplicand if 1, shift, repeat.

items.q: What are the IEEE 754 single fields?

items.a: Its binary fraction repeats forever and must be rounded.
